opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's going to be a hybrid, and the split will be driven less by some grand architectural principle and more by very practical constraints of latency, bandwidth, and what a given deployment can afford.

There's a natural way to think about it that maps onto how people think about their own cognition. Some things need to happen fast. If a robot is folding a shirt or catching something that's slipping out of its gripper, the control loop has to run at tens or hundreds of hertz. You can't route that through a data center halfway across the country, because a few hundred milliseconds of network latency, or a dropped packet, means the shirt is on the floor. So the low-level, reactive part of the policy pretty much has to be onboard.

But a lot of what makes these models capable, like the semantic understanding, the planning, figuring out what "clean up the kitchen" actually means in this particular kitchen, doesn't need to happen at that rate. You can think for a second or two about what to do next, and that kind of slower deliberation can tolerate going off-board to a much bigger model. In our own work we've moved toward architectures where there's a fast action component and a slower, more reasoning-heavy component, and once you have that separation it becomes pretty natural to ask which pieces live where.

On cost, I think people sometimes underestimate how quickly the picture shifts. Onboard compute adds to the bill of materials for every single robot, along with power and heat, whereas off-board compute can be shared and amortized. If you have a fleet of robots that are idle part of the time, centralizing the heavy inference is economically attractive. On the other hand, inference hardware keeps getting cheaper and more efficient, and models get distilled down, so what needed a server rack a couple of years ago might fit on an embedded board soon after.

Connectivity is the wild card. In a factory or warehouse you can engineer a very reliable local network, maybe even put the compute in a closet down the hall, so you get most of the benefits of off-board with almost none of the latency. In a home, or outdoors, or in some agricultural setting, you can't count on that, and you want the robot to degrade gracefully, so it can at least do something sensible and safe if the connection drops.

So my expectation is that we'll see the reactive, safety-critical stuff onboard, the heavy reasoning flexibly placed depending on the environment, and a steady migration of capability onto the robot itself as hardware improves. But I wouldn't bet on either extreme. It's a bit like how your phone does some things locally and some things in the cloud, and nobody really thinks about where the boundary is as long as it works.

r001.rationale: It says off-board compute can be shared and amortized, making heavy inference economically attractive when onboard compute adds cost to every robot.

r002.rationale: It says robots in homes, outdoors, and other settings with unreliable connectivity need to operate sensibly and safely when the connection drops, implying they must retain onboard inference capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of those questions where the answer is less about the technology and more about the economics, and the economics are kind of interesting here.

Right now, if you look at where the big models are, the models that actually have the generality and the robustness you'd want in a robot operating in a home or a warehouse, those are large. They're large in the way that language models are large. And running something like that onboard a robot means you're carrying around a lot of compute, you're spending a lot of power on it, and you're adding cost to every single unit you ship. Whereas if you run it off-board, you amortize that compute across many robots, you can upgrade the model without touching the hardware, and the per-robot cost drops a lot.

So I think the natural equilibrium, at least for the next several years, is a kind of hybrid. You have a fast, relatively small policy running onboard that handles the low-level stuff, the things that need to happen at tens or hundreds of hertz and can't tolerate a network hiccup. Keeping your balance, not crushing the egg, reacting when something slips. And then the heavier reasoning, the "what should I be doing right now, how do I decompose this task," that can live off-board where latency of a few hundred milliseconds is fine. That's roughly how a lot of the current vision-language-action systems are structured anyway, with a big model proposing and a smaller one executing.

Connectivity is the thing that makes people nervous, and I understand why. If your robot is in a kitchen and the WiFi drops, you don't want it to freeze with a knife in its hand. But I'd push back a little on the idea that this is a fundamental obstacle. We already accept this with a lot of devices. Your phone degrades gracefully when it loses signal. And the onboard component can be designed to be safe and conservative on its own, so losing the connection means the robot does something boring, not something dangerous.

The other thing I'd say is that the cost curve on inference is dropping fast, and robots in particular tend to lag behind. So the model that requires a server rack today will probably run on an embedded chip in a few years. Which means the dividing line between what goes onboard and what goes off-board isn't fixed. It keeps moving toward onboard over time, and I think the systems that do well will be the ones designed so you can shift that boundary without re-architecting everything.

If I had to bet, I'd say the first commercially meaningful deployments will lean heavily off-board, partly for cost and partly because you want the data and the ability to iterate on the model centrally. And then as things mature and the models get distilled down, you'll see more and more of it migrate onto the robot. But I don't think "fully onboard" is the goal in itself. The goal is a robot that works, and wherever the compute lives is sort of an implementation detail that follows the economics.

r001.rationale: Predicts early commercially meaningful deployments will lean heavily off-board, citing lower per-robot cost.

r002.rationale: It says onboard control should handle latency-sensitive tasks and remain safe if WiFi drops, but does not predict that robots in unreliable-connectivity settings will use onboard inference.

astra-6.text:
I think it’ll probably be a mix. If you have a reliable connection, there’s a pretty strong economic argument for doing a lot of the computation off-board. You can share a much more powerful computer across many robots, and you don’t have to put all that hardware—and the power and cooling it requires—on every machine.

But you don’t want the robot to become helpless when the connection drops. And there are parts of control where latency matters a lot. If you’re responding to contact or maintaining balance, you probably want that computation onboard. If you’re deciding what to do next, or interpreting a complicated instruction, you can tolerate more delay.

So a natural architecture is to have an onboard system that can handle immediate control and keep the robot operating safely, with a larger off-board system providing more sophisticated reasoning when it’s available. Where you draw that boundary will depend on the application. A robot in a warehouse with good connectivity is in a different situation from one operating somewhere with an unreliable network. And as onboard computation gets cheaper, that boundary can move.

r001.rationale: The response says reliable connectivity creates a strong economic case for off-board computation because powerful hardware can be shared across robots.

r002.rationale: It says onboard systems should handle immediate control and safe operation, and contrasts well-connected robots with those operating on an unreliable network.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’ll probably be a mix. If you have a reliable connection, there’s a pretty strong economic argument for doing the expensive computation off-board. You can share that compute across many robots, and you don’t have to put a powerful computer, with all its power and cooling requirements, into every single machine.

But you don’t want the robot to depend on that connection for everything. If the network drops out, it still needs to behave safely. And for things that require very low latency, like reacting to contact or maintaining balance, you probably want that computation onboard.

So I would expect something hierarchical, where the robot can handle immediate control locally, while more expensive reasoning or planning can happen remotely. Where exactly you draw that boundary will depend on the application, the connectivity, and how the relative costs evolve.

r001.rationale: The response says expensive computation can economically run off-board, shared across robots, avoiding powerful computers in each one—a tentative cost-based prediction.

r002.rationale: It says a robot must remain safe if its network drops and places immediate control locally, supporting onboard computation when connectivity is unreliable.
